title: OpenSearch prereleases carried Shai-Hulud
synopsis: Four @opensearch-project/opensearch prereleases were published with Mini Shai-Hulud malware. OpenSearch removed them and blocked repository writes during credential rotation.
story:
OpenSearch reported the compromise on the evening of May 11, 2026 in America/New_York time. Four prerelease versions of the official `@opensearch-project/opensearch` npm package were published within minutes of each other and removed from npm by 11:00 p.m. EDT.

The affected versions were `3.5.3`, `3.6.2`, `3.7.0`, and `3.8.0`. OpenSearch treated machines that installed or executed those packages between 0000 and 0300 UTC on May 12 as potentially fully compromised, with all local secrets and keys requiring rotation from another system.

The advisory tied the activity to the broader Mini Shai-Hulud campaign against npm and CI/CD publishing infrastructure. JFrog described the campaign's npm payload as a preinstall loader with obfuscated JavaScript that steals credentials, exfiltrates through redundant channels, and uses stolen access to publish more compromised packages.

OpenSearch removed the packages, blocked project repository write permissions, and began credential rotation. This attack record carries the OpenSearch package versions; the campaign record carries the cross-package TeamPCP machinery.

title: node-ipc npm account shipped credential stealer
synopsis: Three malicious node-ipc npm releases were published on 2026-05-14 after the dormant `atiertant` co-maintainer account was recovered via an expired email domain. The obfuscated payload harvested developer, cloud, SSH, and CI/CD secrets and exfiltrated them over DNS TXT queries.
story:
This was a new node-ipc supply-chain event, separate from the 2022 protestware incident. On 2026-05-14 the npm package received three new releases across active and legacy version lines: 12.0.1 at 14:25:30 UTC, 9.2.3 at 14:26:01 UTC, and 9.1.6 at 14:26:25 UTC — all three signed by the dormant co-maintainer `atiertant` inside a 56-second window. Socket traced the entry to expired email domain takeover: the attacker re-registered the lapsed domain behind the maintainer's account, ran a standard npm password reset, and reached publish without touching the project's GitHub repository or any active maintainer's machine. Socket's scanner flagged the publishes within roughly three minutes.

Static comparison against 12.0.0 showed the main ESM file unchanged; an identical 80 KB obfuscated block was appended to `node-ipc.cjs` after the legitimate exports in all three tarballs, making CommonJS consumers the execution path. The payload fired via `setImmediate()` during module load, exported under `__ntRun`, and forked a detached child process with the `__ntw=1` environment marker as both anti-re-execution flag and process tag. The collector swept 113 paths on Linux and 127 on macOS, covering SSH keys, AWS/Azure/GCP credentials, `.npmrc`, `.env` files, Kubernetes and Docker configs, npm tokens, database connection strings, and AI tool configs including `.claude.json` and `.kiro/settings/mcp.json`. It also captured the full `process.env` and host details from `uname` and `/etc/hosts`.

Output was staged under `<tmpdir>/nt-<pid>/`, tarballed with a fixed `1985-10-26` timestamp on every file (a memorable forensic tell), HMAC-signed with the embedded key `qZ8pL3vNxR9wKmTyHbVcFgDsJaEoUi`, and exfiltrated over DNS TXT queries against the `bt.node.js` zone using the prefixes `xh`, `xd`, and `xf` with a custom base-16 reversed-nibble encoding. Bootstrap name resolution went through `sh.azurestaticprovider.net:443` (37.16.75.69), a deliberate Azure-domain masquerade. DNS-only exfiltration bypassed most CI egress controls that would have blocked an outbound HTTPS POST.

The package still looked like node-ipc: name, repository metadata, README, certificates, and API files were all intact. The trust break was in the registry distribution channel, where a fresh install or permissive semver range could resolve to the malicious release without a downstream code review. dist-tags pointed `latest` to 12.0.1, so unversioned installs picked up the malicious build until npm pulled the releases.

title: actions-cool GitHub Actions tags rewritten by TeamPCP
synopsis: TeamPCP re-pointed all 53 issues-helper tags and all 15 maintain-one-comment tags to a single dangling imposter commit on 2026-05-18. The injected step downloaded Bun, scraped Runner.Worker memory for masked secrets, and exfiltrated them to t.m-kosche.com.
story:
`actions-cool/issues-helper` and `actions-cool/maintain-one-comment` are two widely consumed GitHub Actions for triage automation; the issues-helper action alone is referenced by roughly 3,000 public workflow configurations. On 2026-05-18 between 19:10:24 UTC and 19:13:40 UTC the attacker re-pointed every existing tag on both repositories to a single dangling commit. Issues-helper saw all 53 version tags moved in roughly three minutes, and maintain-one-comment had all 15 tags moved inside a 39-second window. The imposter commits had no branch reachability; they sat as orphans labeled `Build action for vX.Y.Z` to imitate legitimate release commits. Any workflow pinning either action by tag (`@v3.8.0`, `@v3.7.6`, etc.) rather than by full commit SHA picked up the malicious code on next run.

The injected action.yaml step downloaded the Bun JavaScript runtime to `/home/runner/.bun/bin/bun`, then spawned a Python process that read the address space of the GitHub Actions `Runner.Worker` process through `/proc/<PID>/mem`. Runner.Worker holds workflow secrets in decrypted form once they are bound to the running job, marked with `"isSecret":true`. The script filtered memory for those markers, extracted the GitHub `GITHUB_TOKEN`, ran `gh auth token` for redundancy, escalated with `sudo python3` where the runner allowed passwordless sudo, and posted the harvested material over HTTPS to `t.m-kosche.com` on port 443. That C2 host is the same OpenTelemetry-trace masquerade endpoint used the same day in the @antv npm wave, the durabletask PyPI publish, and the Nx Console extension publish, tying this Actions tag-rewrite to TeamPCP's broader Mini Shai-Hulud operation.

StepSecurity's Harden-Runner flagged the imposter commits and the runner-memory read pattern, and added `t.m-kosche.com` to its global block list along with a compromised-actions policy that prevents workflow execution against the affected refs. GitHub later disabled both `actions-cool/issues-helper` and `actions-cool/maintain-one-comment` repositories, which removes the malicious tags from new clones but does not retroactively protect workflows that already cached the imposter SHAs in their action runs.

The actions-cool tag-rewrite is the opening move of TeamPCP's 2026-05-18/19 cluster: it ran about five hours before the @antv npm publish wave began at 01:56 UTC on May 19, and the harvested Actions tokens are a plausible source of the credentials Wiz later observed feeding the same-day `nrwl/nx-console` and `microsoft/durabletask-python` compromises. The cross-ecosystem aggregate sits on [[shai-hulud-here-we-go-again]]; this record holds the GitHub Actions evidence.

title: Nx Console VS Code extension shipped credential stealer
synopsis: A compromised contributor published Nx Console 18.95.0 to the VS Code Marketplace and OpenVSX on 2026-05-18. The malicious build fetched an obfuscated payload that harvested Vault, npm, AWS, GitHub, 1Password, and SSH credentials and installed a Python LaunchAgent on macOS.
story:
Nrwl had hardened the npm publish path for `nx` after the August 2025 s1ngularity attack, but Nx Console kept a softer release setup: any single member of the organization could publish a new VS Code extension version without manual approval. On 2026-05-18, an attacker holding a stolen contributor credential used that surface to push a malicious 18.95.0 build to both the Visual Studio Marketplace and OpenVSX.

Nrwl traced the entry point to a developer whose GitHub CLI credentials had been leaked a week earlier by the TanStack `Mini Shai-Hulud` compromise. Those credentials let the attacker run workflows on the Nx Console repository as a contributor and reach the extension publishing path. The build sat on the Visual Studio Marketplace for roughly 18 minutes (12:30 UTC publish to 12:48 UTC unpublish) and on OpenVSX for roughly 36 minutes (12:33 UTC publish to 13:09 UTC unpublish).

The 18.95.0 extension fetched and ran an obfuscated multi-channel stealer. Collectors targeted Vault tokens, `.npmrc` credentials, AWS metadata endpoints and Secrets Manager, GitHub `ghp_`/`gho_`/`ghs_` tokens and Actions secrets, 1Password CLI session contents, and on-disk private keys, connection strings, GCP service accounts, and Docker credentials. Harvested data was exfiltrated over HTTPS, the GitHub API using the victim's own tokens, and DNS. On Linux it attempted sudoers injection; on macOS it dropped `~/.local/share/kitty/cat.py` and registered the LaunchAgent `~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.user.kitty-monitor.plist` for persistence. StepSecurity's analysis also identified a Sigstore abuse module aimed at npm trusted publishing: code paths for requesting Fulcio short-lived certificates from `fulcio.sigstore.dev`, logging to `rekor.sigstore.dev`, and emitting `slsa.dev/provenance/v1` attestations through npm's OIDC trusted-publisher flow. Had harvested OIDC material been used before discovery, the attacker could have published follow-on npm versions carrying legitimate-looking provenance attestations; the 18-to-36-minute exposure window appears to have closed before any such publish landed, but the capability is the architecturally novel piece relative to the August 2025 s1ngularity payload.

Microsoft and OpenVSX reported low official download counts (28 and 41), but Nrwl's internal analytics showed roughly 6,000 18.95.0 activations from VS Code in the two days after the incident. Nrwl shipped a clean 18.100.0, required two-admin manual approval on Nx Console publishes to match the `nx` npm pipeline, and asked users to update, kill any `cat.py` or `__DAEMONIZED` processes, unload the LaunchAgent, delete the persistence files, and rotate every credential reachable from affected machines.

title: AntV ecosystem npm packages hit by TeamPCP
synopsis: TeamPCP used the compromised `atool` npm maintainer account to publish 639 malicious versions across 323 AntV-ecosystem packages on 2026-05-19. Each carried a bun-based dropper that harvested CI/CD secrets and self-propagated via npm.
story:
The @antv ecosystem is Alibaba's open-source data-visualization stack, with libraries such as `@antv/g2`, `@antv/g6`, `@antv/x6`, `@antv/l7`, and `@antv/s2` plus widely depended-on neighbors `echarts-for-react`, `timeago.js`, `size-sensor`, `jest-canvas-mock`, and `jest-date-mock`. On 2026-05-19, TeamPCP compromised the shared `atool` npm maintainer account and used it to publish two coordinated waves of malicious versions: the first at 01:56 UTC and the second at roughly 02:06 UTC, with publish activity continuing until 02:56 UTC. Socket counted 639 malicious package-versions across 323 unique packages; the operation accounted for the bulk of the broader Mini Shai-Hulud day-of total of 1,055 versions across 502 unique packages across npm, PyPI, and Composer.

The published packages used two delivery paths. Most rewrote `package.json` with a `preinstall` or `postinstall` script of `bun run index.js` and shipped an injected root-level `index.js`. A second set added an `optionalDependencies` entry pointing at a poisoned commit in the legitimate `antvis/G2` repository, with a `prepare` hook that ran the same payload under Bun. The 486-498 KB obfuscated payload swept more than 130 on-disk credential paths covering GitHub, npm, AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, HashiCorp Vault, Docker, SSH, and database connection strings, and it specifically read GitHub Actions runner process memory through `/proc/*/mem` to recover masked CI/CD secrets in plaintext.

The payload included npm worm logic: validate the stolen npm token, enumerate every package the victim could publish to, fetch the latest tarball, inject the same dropper, and republish. Exfiltration ran over HTTPS to `t.m-kosche.com:443/api/public/otel/v1/traces` (an OpenTelemetry-trace masquerade using AES-256-GCM with RSA-OAEP key wrapping) with a fallback GitHub dead-drop channel that wrote `results/results-<timestamp>-<counter>.json` files into public repositories created on stolen accounts. Those repos carried the reversed marker description `niagA oG eW ereH :duluH-iahS` and Dune-themed names such as `sayyadina-stillsuit-852`; Socket counted between 2,200 and 2,500 such dead-drop repositories by the end of the day. Persistence injected hooks into `.claude/settings.json`, `.claude/setup.mjs`, `.vscode/tasks.json`, `.vscode/setup.mjs`, and `.github/workflows/codeql.yml`, attempted sudoers injection on Linux, and on macOS dropped the `~/.local/share/kitty/cat.py` Python backdoor and `com.user.kitty-monitor.plist` LaunchAgent shared with the same-day Nx Console compromise.

Socket flagged most malicious versions within 6 to 12 minutes of publish (median 6.7 minutes), and npm classified the affected versions as known malware. Wiz attributed the activity to TeamPCP with moderate confidence based on infrastructure overlap (`t.m-kosche.com`, `firedalazer` dead-drop tag), payload similarities, and reuse of the kitty backdoor and Dune-themed exfiltration repos. The @antv operation also seeded the same-day compromises of [[nx-console]] (VS Code extension) and [[durabletask-pypi]] (Microsoft Azure SDK on PyPI), which used credentials and infrastructure that Wiz tracked back to this account-takeover wave; the cross-ecosystem aggregate sits on [[shai-hulud-here-we-go-again]].

title: Microsoft durabletask PyPI hit by Mini Shai-Hulud
synopsis: TeamPCP published malicious durabletask 1.4.1, 1.4.2, and 1.4.3 to PyPI with a stolen token, bypassing Microsoft's CI/CD path. The dropper fetched rope.pyz to harvest cloud and password-manager credentials, spread via AWS SSM and kubectl, and conditionally wiped disks.
story:
The Microsoft `durabletask` package is the official Python SDK for Azure Durable Functions, with roughly 400,000 monthly PyPI downloads. On 2026-05-19, TeamPCP published three malicious versions (1.4.1, 1.4.2, 1.4.3) within a 35-minute window, then a GitHub issue and Amazon Inspector advisory triggered Microsoft to yank them. None of the three versions had matching tags, releases, or CI/CD runs in the `microsoft/durabletask-python` repository: the attacker reached the registry directly with a stolen publishing credential, bypassing the project's GitHub path. Wiz attributed the entry to a compromised contributor account previously linked to the `@antv` wave; the attacker copied the latest legitimate commit message to mask the upload and extracted the PyPI token from GitHub repository secrets.

Each version pushed the dropper into more package entry points: 1.4.1 patched `__init__.py`; 1.4.2 added `task.py`; 1.4.3 spread across `entities/`, `extensions/`, and `payload/` `__init__.py` files. The 14-line dropper executed at import time on Linux only and pulled a 28 KB second stage, `rope.pyz`, from `check.git-service.com` (registered three days earlier via NameSilo). The second stage targeted 90+ on-disk credential paths covering AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, HashiCorp Vault, GitHub, Docker, SSH, Terraform/Ansible/Pulumi state, shell histories, AI tool configs (Claude, Cursor, VS Code MCP, Codeium), and the 1Password, Bitwarden, `pass`, and `gopass` CLIs. Persistence dropped `/tmp/managed.pyz`, installed a `pgsql-monitor.service` systemd unit, and marked infected hosts via `~/.cache/.sys-update-check`.

Propagation matched TeamPCP's other 2026 waves: AWS SSM `SendCommand` against up to five EC2 instances per harvested profile, and `kubectl exec` into up to five pods per discovered cluster. Exfiltration ran three parallel channels — HTTPS POST to the C2, GitHub commit beacons under the `FIRESCALE` tag using victim tokens, and public repos created on stolen GitHub accounts using Russian-folklore names (BABA-YAGA, KOSCHEI, FIREBIRD, RUSALKA, MOROZKO, LESHY). Evasion checks excluded Russian-locale systems and hosts with two or fewer CPU cores, and silenced all output to `/dev/null`. A `roulette.py` module inspected locale settings for Israeli and Iranian targets and, when matched, played an audio file and ran `rm -rf /*` with a 1-in-6 probability.

Amazon Inspector flagged the packages as MAL-2026-4174 and a public report landed in `microsoft/durabletask-python` issue #137 at 17:54 UTC; Microsoft yanked all three versions ten minutes later. The shared `t.m-kosche.com` infrastructure and reused folklore-naming pattern tied the operation to TeamPCP's Mini Shai-Hulud activity, even though `durabletask` was PyPI rather than npm and the payload was a Python `pyz` rather than the `@tanstack/setup` Node module used in the May 11 wave. This record holds the durabletask-specific evidence; the cross-ecosystem aggregate stays on [[shai-hulud-here-we-go-again]].
